content.title: Thank you for your review-Part1
content.comment:
Thank you for your review. Due to the character limitation, please find our part1 answers below.

**Weakness1**

Please provide more details about why you think the design of the personalized augmentation selector is trivial so that we can explain it to you.

The main goal of this paper is to bridge the research gap in GCL by allocating personalized augmentation strategies to different samples in the dataset. This is pretty novel and new to the whole contrastive learning community even for methods in computer vision. Like JOAO, we follow the precious GCL protocol to set the contrastive learning part to make our proposal generable. To tackle this personalized augmentation problem, we aim to build a simple but effective technique at this moment. The idea is to convert the discrete selection into a continuous learnable way, which is inspired by the popular neural architecture search work in DARTs[1]. However, there exists a critical difference between them. Standard DARTs focus on directly learning a set of weight vectors for each component, but this solution cannot be directly applicable to our case because of two reasons. First, if we assign a $K$-dimensional weight vector to each graph following DARTs, then the total trainable parameters would be $K\times |\mathcal{G}|$, which is linear to the size of the dataset $\mathcal{G}$. Such huge parameters are challenging to optimize. Second, directly assigning a trainable vector to each graph is transductive, so the model cannot allocate personalized augmentations to unseen graphs during the training, which limits its applications in practice. To tackle this problem, we propose to parameterize the selector as a neural network and leverage the topology structure and node attributes of a graph to predict its sampling distribution. This approximation is new to DARTs and GCL.  To summarize, we propose an elegant solution to tackle a new and challenging problem in GCL. It provides crucial modifications to existing ideas and enjoys simplicity and wide applicability. 

[1] Liu, Hanxiao, et al. DARTS: Differentiable Architecture Search,. ICLR, 2019. 

**Weakness2**

The performance of GPA is definitely obvious compared with the relative baselines. As discussed in Section5, the most relevant baselines to us are GraphCL and JOAO, since other baseline methods such as AD-GCL and AutoGCL belong to the view generation-based approach. We highlight the comparison between GPA and non-generation-based baselines in the table below. From the table, we can observe that GPA generally outperformed the strong baseline --JOAO by a wide margin.

|          | JOAOv2 | GPA   | Improvement  |
|----------|--------|-------|--------------:|
| NCI1     | 78.36  | 80.42 | **+2.06**        |
| PROTEINS | 74.07  | 75.94 | **+1.87**        |
| DD       | 77.4   | 79.9  | **+2.50**        |
| MUTAG    | 87.67  | 89.68 | **+2.01**        |
| COLLAB   | 69.33  | 76.17 | **+6.84**       |
| RDT-B    | 86.42  | 89.32 | **+2.90**        |
| IMDB-B   | 70.83  | 74.64 | **+3.81**        |

AD-GCL and AutoGCL belong to the type: GCL with view generation. Ordinarily, they should not be considered as our baselines since GPA belongs to GCL with augmentation selection, not view generation. Please note that GPA does not add a component to them. They are entirely different types of work. As shown in Table 2&3, compared with view-generation-based methods such as AD-GCL and AutoGCL, our model GPA could still achieve very competitive results across different scenarios by ranking top 1 on average. It is worth noting that GPA is the first augmentation-selection based approach that could achieve comparable results with view-generation-based methods. This is a big achievement for the augmentation-selection based approach because it indicates the effectiveness of augmentation strategies defined by domain experts.

content.title: Thank you for your review-Part2
content.comment:
Thank you for your review. Due to the character limitation, please find our part2 answers below.

**Weakness3**

For a bi-level optimization, we need to first train the lower-level optimization until convergence to find the optimal solution, and then use this solution to optimize the upper-level. “one step of gradient descent update for w” targets to approximate the optimal solution without training the lower-level optimization until convergence that is intractable and computationally expensive. 
Due to the page limitation, equation (7) is the final result.  The full derivation process is left in Appendix C.

**Weakness4**

Thanks for your comments. We agree with the reviewer that it is always better to provide algorithms with a theoretical guarantee. However, the research process often starts from empirical observations to theoretically understand, such as the path to understanding the expressive power of graph neural networks. The development of GCL faces the same issue too because it is pretty hard to provide even an interpretable understanding of the impact of data augmentation on graphs, nor a theoretical proof. We believe it is still in the early stage of contrastive learning on graphs. That’s why we only provide empirical validation and visualization in this paper following standard GCL methods, such as GraphCL and JOAO.  We leave the theoretical understanding of personalized augmentation allocation as our future work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studied graph contrastive learning (GCL) in the label scarcity scenario. Motivated by the phenomenon that different graphs might need diverse augmentations to perform effective GCL, the paper proposed personalized graph augmentation to consider the individual characteristics of each graph. To achieve this, they designed a tailored augmentation selector by converting the discrete space into continuous and introduced a bi-level framework to optimize the encoder and augmentation selector alternatively. Extensive experiments on ten benchmarks are performed to verify the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
For strengths, I agree it’s interesting and reasonable to introduce the personalized augmentation problem. The problem is well formulated and motivated, and most of the paper is well-written and easy to follow. In addition, the method part is sound, and the bi-level framework introduced does have the potential to optimize the model well. Many datasets are also selected to perform the evaluation.

For weaknesses, the technical novelty is limited. The main algorithm is similar to the bi-level optimization framework in JOAO, and the difference is just that they relax the data set-level augmentation to sample-level. 

Moreover, the method needs to iterate through all possible augmentation combinations and forward-backward them to optimize the model. The bi-level optimization framework will also increase the training time. The time consumption of the proposed algorithm is also one of my major concerns.

For evaluation, one important baseline about automated and personalized augmentation is missing. [1] also proposed a learnable generator to perform augmentation for each graph. In addition, current experiments are only conducted on graph-level tasks. Is the method able to generalize to node-level tasks? In that setting, does the proposed personalized augmentation degrade to dataset-level augmentation? Another point is that though its intuitive personalized augmentation has the potential to perform better than dataset-level augmentation, it’s better to justify and compare those empirically or theoretically. The paper only provided the visualization of the learned personalized augmentation distribution now, which I think is not enough.

Besides, some notations are not very clear. For example, L(G_n) in equation 5 can lead to misunderstandings. It makes me feel the loss is irrelevant to the graph augmentations. In the appendix, $\alpha$ in equation 9 should be $\theta$, one comma is missing in equation 10.

[1] Bringing Your Own View: Graph Contrastive Learning without Prefabricated Data Augmentations. WSDM 2022.

content.title: Thank you for your review-Part1
content.comment:
Thank you for your review. Due to the character limitation, please find our part1 answers below.

**Technical Novelty**

The main goal of this paper is to bridge the research gap in GCL by allocating personalized augmentation strategies to different samples in the dataset. This is pretty novel and new to the whole contrastive learning community even for methods in computer vision. While JOAO and GPA all focus on training GraphCL in an automated fashion, they differ in two crucial ways: 1) The research problem is different. JOAO aims to learn a shared sampling distribution for a given dataset, but GPA targets to learn a sampling vector for each instance (i.e., graph) in the dataset. Notably, due to randomness, JOAO can sample different augmentations to different graphs to some extent. However, since the sampling distribution is fixed, it is “fake” personalization because it does not consider the characteristics of different graphs. In contrast, GPA could explicitly generate personalized sampling distribution to each graph, which is tailored and more challenging as the augmentation space grows exponentially to the dataset size. 2) The sampler optimization process is different. JOAO adopts a sampling-based approach to directly train a $K$-dimensional sampling distribution parameters. However, such a solution cannot be applied to our personalized scenarios because i) the total trainable parameters will be linear to the size of the dataset, i.e., $K\times |\mathcal{V}|$, where $\mathcal{V}$ is the dataset; and ii) it is restricted to transductive settings and cannot generate distribution vectors for new graphs, i.e., unseen graphs during training. To this end, we adopt a new approach to achieve personalized augmentation allocation by parameterizing the sampler as a neural network taking the topological and node attributes of a graph as input. It reduces the trainable parameters of the sampler to be independent of the size of the dataset. It is also worth mentioning that the performance gap between JOAO and GPA is huge as shown in Table2&3.

**Time Consumption**

We analyzed the running cost of JOAO and GPA. Please note that our search space(15^(num of graphs in a dataset)) is actually much larger than JOAO's (only 15). To avoid randomness, we report the averaged results of 10 epochs under the same setting on a platform with GTX1650 Ti. The results are shown below. 
|  | JOAO  |  GPA   | Times(GPA/JOAO)  |
|  :-----  | ----:  |----: |----:  |
| MUTAG  | 1.07 | 7.46 | 6.99 |
| PROTEINS  | 5.80 | 70.63 | 12.18 |
| NCI1  | 110.38 | 193.89 | 1.76 |
| Average  |  |  | 6.97 |

From the table, we observe that, on average, the running time of GPA is 6.97 times slower than JOAO. Compared with the huge gap of search space between GPA and JOAO(15^(num_of_graphs) vs. 15), we believe GPA’s running complexity is tolerable. Besides, please note that the optimization process of JOAO is not efficient because it requires alternatively updating K sampling probabilities. As shown in their code, in each epoch, JOAO needs to go through the whole dataset K times in order to update the K-dimensional sampling vector.  When the dataset is large, its running time might increase significantly. In summary, given the huge gap of search space between GPA and JOAO and their obvious performance gap in Table 2&3, GPA’s running complexity is acceptable.

**Bringing Your Own View: LP**

Thanks for your reference. We cited this paper in the updated related work section. As we discussed in Section 3.5, the suggested work still belongs to the view generation approach, which aims to learn a graph generator rather than an augmentation selector.  These works are not directly related to us since GPA focuses on augmentation selection. JOAO is the only related work in the literature.  However, to provide a comprehensive comparison, we include two representative generation methods:  AD-GCL and AutoGCL. Notably, they are the SOTA methods in generation approach and consistently perform better than the suggested work according to their empirical results. Also, the performance in Table2&3 shows that GPA performs better or on par with AD-GCL and AutoGCL. We highlight the comparison between your proposed baseline and GPA in the following table to eliminate your concern.

|     | RDT-B | RDT-M5K | GITHUB  |
|-----|-------|---------|---------|
| LP  | 88.03 | 53.32   | 63.11   |
| GPA | **89.99** | **54.92**   | **68.31**   |

content.comment:
Thank you for your review. Due to the character limitation, please find our part2 answers below.

**Graph-level to Node-level**

While we focus on graph-level tasks, node-level tasks could also suffer from the personalization augmentation issue, since the performance of node-level SOTA methods such as BGRL/MVGRL[1,2], is shown to be sensitive to the choice of augmentation strategies. In light of this, our proposal is applicable to node-level tasks too. However, it might be a non-trivial application because node-level contrastive learning baselines are often trained with full batch training, which may be memory-demanding when considering personalized augmentation.

[1] Thakoor, Shantanu, et al. Large-scale representation learning on graphs via bootstrapping, ICLR, 2022.

[2] Hassani, Kaveh, et al. Contrastive Multi-View Representation Learning on Graphs, ICML, 2020.

**Theoretical Understanding**

Although it is always better to provide algorithms with a theoretical guarantee, the research process often starts from empirical observations to theoretically understand, such as the path to understanding the expressive power of graph neural networks. GCL faces the same issue too because it is pretty hard to provide even an interpretable understanding of the impact of data augmentation on graphs, nor a theoretical proof. We believe it is still in the early stage of contrastive learning on graphs. That’s why we only provide empirical validation and visualization in this paper following standard GCL methods, such as GraphCL and JOAO.  We leave the theoretical understanding of personalized augmentation allocation as our future work.

**Notation Fix**

Thank you for your detailed review. We have corrected the equations.

content.title: Thank you for your review-Part1
content.comment:
Thank you for your review. Due to the character limitation, please find our part1 answers below.

**Difference between JOAO and GPA**

While JOAO and GPA all focus on training GraphCL in an automated fashion, they differ in two crucial ways: 1) **The research problem is different.** JOAO aims to learn a shared sampling distribution for a given dataset, but GPA targets to learn a sampling vector for each instance (i.e., graph) in the dataset. Notably, due to randomness, JOAO can sample different augmentations to different graphs to some extent. However, it is a “fake” personalization because the sampling distribution vector is shared for all graphs. In contrast, GPA could explicitly generate personalized sampling distribution to each graph, which is tailored and more challenging as the augmentation space grows exponentially to the number of graphs in a dataset. 2) **The sampler optimization process is different.** JOAO adopts a sampling-based approach to directly train a $K$-dimensional sampling distribution parameters. However, such a solution cannot be applied to our personalized scenarios because i) the total trainable parameters will be linear to the size of a dataset, i.e., $K\times |\mathcal{V}|$, where $\mathcal{V}$ is the dataset, which is not only too large to be trained in practice in large-scale scenarios. Moreover, it is also difficult to optimize the distribution parameters because they are totally independent of each other, i.e., each distribution vector only has one training sample to fit; and ii) it is restricted to transductive settings and cannot generate distribution vectors for new graphs, i.e., unseen graphs during training. To this end, we adopt a new approach to achieve personalized augmentation allocation by parameterizing the sampler as a neural network taking the topological and node attributes of a graph as input. It reduces the trainable parameters of the sampler to be independent of the size of the dataset.

**Methodology Novelty**

We follow the precious GCL protocol to set the contrastive learning part to make our proposal generable. To tackle this personalized augmentation problem, we aim to build a simple but effective technique at this moment. The idea is to convert the discrete selection into a continuous learnable way, which is inspired by the popular neural architecture search work in DARTs[1]. However, there exists a critical difference between them. Standard DARTs focus on directly learning a set of weight vectors for each component, but this solution cannot be directly applicable to our case because of two reasons. **First**, if we assign a $K$-dimensional weight vector to each graph following DARTs, then the total trainable parameters would be $K\times |\mathcal{G}|$, which is linear to the size of the dataset $\mathcal{G}$. Such huge parameters are challenging to optimize. **Second**, directly assigning a trainable vector to each graph is transductive, so the model cannot allocate personalized augmentations to unseen graphs during the training, which limits its applications in practice. To tackle this problem, we propose to parameterize the selector as a neural network and leverage the topology structure and node attributes of a graph to predict its sampling distribution. This approximation is new to DARTs and GCL.  **To summarize, we propose an elegant solution to tackle a new and challenging problem in GCL. It provides crucial modifications to existing ideas and enjoys simplicity and wide applicability.**

[1]  Liu, Hanxiao, et al. DARTS: Differentiable Architecture Search,ICLR, 2019.

**Typos in point1 of Clarity**

Thank you for pointing this out. This sentence means that after the selector is plugged in, we can adopt it to train the GCL model. We have modified it to be more clear in the revised version

**Why not Reinforcement Learning**

Reinforcement learning is often defined over a discrete and non-differentiable search space, so the training of reinforcement learning is notorious for being data hungry, i.e., it requires sampling a lot of data to have a well-trained selector. This data-hungry property is suboptimal to our personalized allocation problem since its potential search space is exponential to the size of the dataset. Accelerating the training speed is the driving force to not consider reinforcement learning in our problem. In fact, the inefficiency issue of reinforcement learning has been widely verified in the neural architecture search domain, which also faces the discrete selection problem but has a relatively smaller search space than ours. In contrast, by converting the discrete search space into a continuous space, bi-level optimization can be utilized to train the selector via gradient descent effectively. We have simply illustrated this in the third paragraph of Section3.2

content.title: Thank you for your review-Part2
content.comment:
Thank you for your review. Due to the character limitation, please find our part2 answers below.

**The scenario that the test data has a huge gap with the validation data**

Thanks for your insightful comments. How to address the distribution shift between the training set and testing set is still an open challenge. In this work, we only focus on the same distribution assumption following previous GCL works. We leave the distribution shift problem as our future work.

**Time complexity**

GraphCL performs contrastive learning on the dataset level without an automatic selection mechanism. Thus, to obtain the well-established GraphCL model from scratch, we need to conduct a grid search on the augmentation space, which is 15 for dataset-level scenarios and 15^(# of graphs) for graph-level scenarios. The reasonable baseline for GPA is JOAO, since they all focus on avoiding the tedious grid-search using automated selection. Notably, JOAO still focuses on learning a unified sampling distribution to select the optimal augmentations for the whole dataset but GPA aims to learn a personalized sampling distribution to find the best augmentation for individual graphs. 

To further address your concern, we analyzed the running cost of JOAO and GPA. Please note that our search space(15^(num of graphs in a dataset)) is actually much larger than JOAO's (only 15). To avoid randomness, we report the averaged results of 10 epochs under the same setting on a platform with GTX1650 Ti. The results are shown below. 
|  | JOAO  |  GPA   | Times(GPA/JOAO)  |
|  :-----  | ----:  |----: |----:  |
| MUTAG  | 1.07 | 7.46 | 6.99 |
| PROTEINS  | 5.80 | 70.63 | 12.18 |
| NCI1  | 110.38 | 193.89 | 1.76 |
| Average  |  |  | 6.97 |

From the table, we observe that, on average, the running time of GPA is 6.97 times slower than JOAO. Compared with the huge gap of search space between GPA and JOAO(15^(num_of_graphs) vs. 15), we believe GPA’s running complexity is tolerable. Besides, please note that the optimization process of JOAO is not efficient because it requires alternatively updating K sampling probabilities. As shown in their code, in each epoch, JOAO needs to go through the whole dataset K times in order to update the K-dimensional sampling vector.  When the dataset is large, its running time might increase significantly. In summary, given the huge gap of search space between GPA and JOAO and their obvious performance gap in Table 2&3, GPA’s running complexity is acceptable.

Besides, please note that the optimization process of JOAO is not efficient because it requires alternatively updating K sampling probabilities. As shown in their code, in each epoch, JOAO needs to go through the whole dataset K times in order to update the K-dimensional sampling vector.  When the dataset is large, its running time might increase significantly. In summary, given the huge gap of search space between GPA and JOAO and their obvious performance gap in Table 2&3, GPA’s running complexity is acceptable.

**Learning Criteria**

How to systematically determine the hyperparameters of contrastive learning, such as training epochs and learning rate, is still an open question. We follow the standard learning criteria of GraphCL and conduct a grid search on these hyperparameters. Specifically, we search the number of epochs from set {10,20,30} and the learning rate from {0.01,0.001,0.0001,0.00001,0.000001}. To avoid randomness, we repeat the process ten times and report the average results.

**Reproducibility**

For the unstable results, the shared code only includes the implementation of our model, but the detailed hyperparameter configurations are not attached at this moment. We will release a reproducible configuration after being accepted. To address your concern on PROTEINS performance, you can try the following reproducible script, which reaches 75.92 performance based on our test.

content.title: Runtime efficiency is unsatisfactory
content.comment: I appreciate the authors' response. However, considering the marginal performance improvement which needs a sophisticated parameter-tuning (in practice, we do not have test data for tuning the best parameters in general), the current runtime efficiency is far from satisfactory. In fact, JOAO is not an efficient GCL method. Your method is even slower than it, which is unacceptable in practice IMHO.
